To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NSAIDs and chemoprevention agents regulate the expression of a large number of genes that may be critical to their chemo-preventative activity.
NSAIDs and chemoprevention agents alter gene expression in a COX-2-independent manner and this may be the basis of their chemo-preventative activity.
NSAIDs inhibit the expression of a variety of genes that influence tumorigenesis and that NAG-1 is an important target of NSAIDs and other cancer chemopreventives.
In summary, our research is concerned with

identifying genes that are altered in response to COX inhibition and/or other chemopreventative agents, determining the mechanisms by which these genes are regulated and the functional significance of their altered expression.
the identification of genes regulated by COX-1 and/or COX-2 inhibition and how these genes contribute to chemoprevention by COX inhibitors.
the mechanisms by which NSAIDs and other chemopreventives inhibit tumorigenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the chemoprevention of cancer by COX inhibitors is a multi-factorial process involving COX inhibition, altered gene expression, and other mechanisms.
COX inhibitors have a chemoprotective effect on cancer development, in part, via the regulation of gene expression.
NSAIDs and other chemopreventives alter gene expression, including the expression of NAG-1, and that this is an important factor in cancer prevention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemoprevention by NSAIDs may be due, in part, to altered gene expression
NSAIDs have multiple mechanisms of action that may contribute to their anti-cancer activity.
the chemoprevention of cancer by COX inhibitors may be mediated by a number of mechanisms, including the inhibition of COX activity and/or the induction of gene expression.

the chemoprevention of cancer by COX inhibitors may be due, in part, to their ability to alter gene expression

the COX-independent chemopreventative effects of NSAIDs are due to the ability of these drugs to alter gene expression, and this effect is not unique to NSAIDs but is shared by other cancer-preventive chemicals.
